# Basic mathematics

Mathematics forms the foundation of all quantitative methods. Because this entire book focuses on quantitative applications, starting with these foundational concepts is a natural choice. Some readers may prefer to skip this chapter—or specific parts of it—and return only when notation or concepts in later chapters need clarification.

The practical value of mathematics is a frequent target of humor (such as jokes asking whether knowing the square root of 25 has ever helped in a crisis). Math phobia^[an intense, persistent feeling of tension, apprehension, or fear that interferes with a person's ability to manipulate numbers and solve math problems in daily life or academic settings] is a real experience, and many people resonate with these jokes.

These jokes often unconsciously reinforce the idea that math is really difficult and useless. Mathematical could loosely fall into four categories:

- easy and useful in everyday life, such as basic arithmetic
- difficult and useless for daily tasks, such as proving Fermat's last theorem
- difficult and highly useful, such as partial differential equations
- easy and largely useless, such as manually calculating $\pi$ to arbitrary precision

The goal of this section is to stay in the realm of the easy and useful, presenting simplified concepts that---hopefully and with perseverance---speak to ecologists and scientists alike.

Most chapters in this section are designed to support upcoming applied topics:

- The opening chapters review fundamental rules of arithmetic (@sec-arithmeticMath) and introduce common Greek letters alongside their standard usage (@sec-greek).
- The distinction between discrete and continuous variables is established (@sec-discreteContinuous), forming a basis for subsequent statistics and programming sections.
- Compact notations for summations and products are explained (@sec-sum), which will be used throughout.
- Matrix definitions and operations are covered across three dedicated chapters (@sec-matrixMath, @sec-matrixOperationMath, and @sec-matrixMultiplicationMath).

The remainder of the section focuses on functions and calculus:

- Functions are formally redefined with an emphasis on domain and codomain (@sec-functionMath).
- Visual interpretations of graphs (@sec-functionViz) and rates of change via the derivative (@sec-derivative) are explored.
- Exponential and logarithmic functions are introduced (@sec-exponential and @sec-log).
- The section concludes by framing dynamic change through difference equations (@sec-difference) and differential equations (@sec-differential).

Because this section covers basic mathematical foundations, R code is intentionally excluded; programming begins in the dedicated. While mathematicians might object to the simplified definitions and visual intuitions, the goal is to strike a practical balance where a reduction in rigor significantly increases accessibility.
